subject: Business Models
title: Wirecard: Europe's Enron
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Wirecard: Europe's Enron.

hook.text: Wirecard was a German fintech in the DAX 30 index. $2 billion of its cash didn't exist.

buildup.text: Wirecard processed payments for merchants, reporting explosive revenue growth that attracted global investors.

discovery.text: Auditors discovered that $2 billion in bank accounts in the Philippines was fabricated. The money was never there.

twist.text: The Financial Times reported the fraud years before the collapse. German regulators investigated the FT, not Wirecard.

climax.text: Wirecard's CEO was arrested. Its COO vanished and is still missing. $2B gone from a regulated public company.

punchline.text: DAX 30, $2B missing. Regulators investigated the journalists, not the fraud.

quiz.question: What happened when the Financial Times reported Wirecard's fraud?
options: German regulators investigated the FT instead of Wirecard

details.summary: Wirecard, a German payment processor valued at 24 billion euros, fabricated 1.9 billion euros in cash balances across Asian bank accounts. When auditor EY could not confirm the funds existed, the company collapsed in days, revealing that billions in reported revenue came from fake transactions.
details.whyItMatters: Wirecard showed that even publicly listed, audited companies in regulated industries can sustain massive fraud for years. It exposed failures in auditing, financial regulation, and short-seller suppression across European financial oversight systems.
takeaways: 1.9 billion euros in reported cash balances simply did not exist
German regulators investigated short-sellers instead of the fraud itself
The collapse wiped out 24 billion euros in market value virtually overnight

faq.question: How did Wirecard maintain the fraud for so long?
faq.answer: Third-party partners in Asia supposedly processed transactions and held funds, making direct verification difficult. Wirecard aggressively attacked journalists and short-sellers who raised questions. German financial regulator BaFin sided with Wirecard, even banning short selling of its stock.

faq.question: What regulatory changes resulted from the Wirecard scandal?
faq.answer: Germany overhauled BaFin with new oversight powers and leadership. Audit reform increased scrutiny of payment processing companies. The European Union accelerated plans for integrated financial supervision. Companies must now provide more transparent third-party partner disclosures.
